core: The typeface-versus-font distinction: a typeface is the design, a font is a specific instance (size/weight/style), with the metal-type origin and the digital-era blurring of the two words
Type anatomy guide lines: baseline, x-height, cap height
Type anatomy strokes and spaces: ascender, descender, stem, bowl, counter, serif (and sans serif as 'without'), terminal
Measurement in points (1/72 inch) and picas (12 points, about 1/6 inch), and that point size measures the slot/body, not the visible letter, so equal point sizes can look different in size
Kerning: adjusting space between one specific pair of letters (e.g., AV, To, Wa)
Tracking (letter-spacing): adjusting space uniformly across a run of text
Leading: vertical space between lines, measured baseline to baseline, named for lead strips, commonly about 120 percent of point size
Legibility (distinguishing characters, a property of the typeface) versus readability (ease of reading connected text, a property of arrangement)
supporting: Highly legible text typefaces tend to have a large x-height, open counters, and low stroke contrast
Body text typically runs roughly 8 to 16 points, with 10 to 12 points common for long reading
The metal-type font as a physical case of one size/weight/style; the shorthand 'Times New Roman is a typeface, Times New Roman 12pt Bold is a font'
outOfScope: Typeface classification into serif, sans serif, slab serif, script, and other categories (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:typeface-classification); serif vs sans is named here only as anatomy
Typographic hierarchy, type pairing, and the type scale (owned by graphic-design-and-digital-media:foundations:typography-hierarchy)
Layout, grids, and composition beyond naming that picas measure column widths
Web/CSS type mechanics (rem/em, font-face loading, variable fonts) and font licensing/rights of specific fonts

claims.claim: A typeface is the design of a family of letters, while a font is a specific instance of that typeface; for example, Times New Roman is a typeface and 'Times New Roman, 12 pt, Bold' is a font.

Historically a font was one physical set of cast type at a single size, weight, and style; in digital use a single scalable file serves all sizes, so 'font' now commonly names the file and the two terms are often used interchangeably.

The baseline is the line the bodies of letters rest on; the x-height is the height of a lowercase x (excluding ascenders and descenders); the cap height is the height of the capital letters from the baseline. An ascender rises above the x-height (b, d, k, t) and a descender drops below the baseline (g, p, q, y).

A counter is the enclosed or partly enclosed white space within a letter; a serif is a small finishing stroke at the end of a main stroke, and type without serifs is called sans serif; a terminal is the end of a stroke that has no serif; a stem is a main/dominant stroke and a bowl is a curved stroke enclosing a rounded space.

Type is measured in points and picas: the point is 1/72 of an inch (and 1/12 of a pica), and the pica is about 1/6 of an inch (12 points). The point originally described the metal body a character was cast on.

Point size does not guarantee consistent visual sizing across typefaces; two faces set at the same point size can look different in size, because point size measures the body/slot rather than the visible letter, and x-height varies between typefaces.
Kerning is the adjustment of space between a specific pair of characters (such as AV, To, or Wa) to even out awkward gaps or collisions; it is distinct from tracking.
Tracking (letter-spacing) uniformly adjusts the horizontal space between all characters across a selected run of text, rather than a single pair.

Leading is the vertical space between lines of text, measured from one baseline to the next; the name comes from lead strips set between lines of metal type. A common default is about 120 percent of the point size (e.g., 10-point type with 12-point leading), with body text often between roughly 120 and 145 percent.

Legibility and readability are distinct: legibility is how easily one character can be distinguished from another (a property of the typeface/glyph design), while readability is how comfortably connected text can be read over time (a property of how the type is arranged). Highly legible text faces tend to have a large x-height, open counters, and low stroke contrast.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strictly the typeface/font distinction should be enforced given that digital tools and everyday designers use the terms interchangeably.
positions: Traditional/precise usage: a typeface is the design and a font is one specific size/weight/style instance, a distinction rooted in metal type.

Practical digital usage: because one scalable file serves all sizes, 'font' commonly means the installed file and both terms are used loosely; the Typography Handbook explicitly notes one need not be pedantic about the terms.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the precise historical distinction as the reason the words exist, then states plainly that the digital era blurred the line and that font and typeface are now often used interchangeably, so students recognize both the correct distinction and common loose usage.

sourceRecords.title: Typography Handbook (chapters: Frequently Used Terms, Clarifying Confusing Terms, Measurements, Anatomy)
sourceRecords.notes: Dedicated open typography handbook. Measurements chapter states the pica is about 1/6 of an inch and the point is 1/72 of an inch or 1/12 of a pica, originally based on the metal body size, and warns that point size does not guarantee consistent sizing across typefaces. Frequently Used Terms defines tracking (uniform spacing across a selection), kerning (spacing between individual characters, e.g., the AV pair), and leading (baseline to baseline; standard 120 percent of point size, realistic body range 120-145 percent), and notes highly legible text faces have a large x-height, open counters, and low stroke contrast. The Clarifying Confusing Terms chapter frames the typeface/font and legibility/readability distinctions and notes one need not be pedantic.
